newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Austerity-minded Pakistan orders simple weddings.
newsitem.headline: Austerity-minded Pakistan orders simple weddings.

text.p: Pakistan's new government has banned lavish wedding banquets in a bid to enforce austerity in a move welcomed by several newspapers on Monday.

A presidential ordinance promulgated at the weekend banned the serving of meals at wedding feasts held in hotels or marriage halls for the next two years. It also prohibited firework displays, firing in the air and street illuminations.
"As a third world country, Pakistan can ill afford wasteful expenditure on marriages," the English-language daily The Frontier Post said in an editorial.
But it voiced concern that the wealthy could circumvent the spirit of the ordinance by holding extravagant wedding feasts in their own homes, where the food restrictions do not apply.
The Nation, a Lahore-based daily, said ostentation at weddings had been carried to "absurd lengths" fuelled by a flood of black money circulating in the economy.

"This display of vulgar wealth has no doubt contributed in some measure to the feelings of envy and bitterness amongst citizens not so 'blessed' as those who have made marriages lengthy affairs involving at times months of ceremonies."
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's attempt to rein in conspicuous consumption has not pleased everyone, particularly hotel managers, caterers and other food suppliers.

"Our business will be affected by at least 10 to 20 percent," said Rehan Abbasi, manager of Islamabad's Usmania Restaurant. "It will be a substantial loss," he said, adding that he would have to lay off some staff.
A manager at a five-star hotel in Islamabad said the ban would not affect his business too badly because the hotel made more profit from renting the hall than from the food served.
A civil servant, planning the wedding of his son next month, said he would defy the ban on food. "I will serve one dish, but only one dish," he said, asking not to be named.
Mussarat Leghari, a columnist in the Urdu-language Nawa-i-Waqt newspaper, said Sharif should have consulted women before taking drastic action to curb wedding spending.
She argued that it would impose hardship on guests coming from far away or staying overnight for the various ceremonies that a traditional Pakistani wedding entails.

"Weddings are the only festival in villages that allow people to relax and enjoy themselves. They save for the entire year to feast their guests," she wrote. "There are certain traditions that cannot and should not be given up suddenly."
